3.15.m: Nārada said: / What you ask me, O son of Kuntī, understand that and hear that: / in the meantime, Rudra stationed himself on the bank of the Narmadā.
At the place named Hareśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds, / in that place Mahādeva reflected on the destruction of the three cities.
Making Mount Mandara his bow, making Vāsuki the bowstring, / adopting the vaiśākha posture, and making Viṣṇu the excellent arrow,
establishing Agni at the tip and assigning Vāyu to the face [of the arrow], / and the four Vedas as the horses, [he formed] a chariot made of all the gods.
The two Aśvin gods stood on the wheels, and the wielder of the discus was himself the axle; / Indra himself stood at the end of the bow, and Vaiśravaṇa on the arrow.
Yama was in his right hand, and fierce Time was in his left; / on the spokes of the wheels were placed the Gandharvas renowned in the world.
Prajāpati was on that excellent chariot, and Brahmā was indeed the charioteer; / having thus made a chariot consisting of all the gods, the lord of gods
stood indeed motionless like a pillar for a thousand solar years, / until the three [cities] traveling in the sky came together.
Then with a three-pronged arrow he pierced those three cities; / the arrow was discharged there by Rudra against Tripura.
The three [cities] became bereft of luster, and their strength dissolved away; / and portents arose by the thousands in that city.
Then, for the destruction of Tripura, he assumed the form of Death; / wooden figures burst into raucous laughter.
And [painted statues] blinked and opened their eyes by wonderful magic; / in dreams, they saw themselves adorned in red garments.
And in dreams they saw things turned upside down in this way. / Whichever people residing there beheld these portents,
their strength and intellect were destroyed by Hara's wrath. / The wind named Saṃvartaka, great and like the end of a cosmic age,
blew; that excellent fire tormented [them] in their heads. / Trees blazed there, and mountain peaks fell.
Everything there became agitated, unconscious, crying out in dismay. / All the gardens were shattered and quickly flared up.
Kindled by that alone, everything blazed with arrow-like flames— / trees, grove clusters, and varied houses.
In the ten directions, this kindled fire set to work; / then rocks were hurled across the ten directions in divisions.
With thousands of exceedingly terrible crests, fires blazed; / the entire city appeared ablaze, resembling kiṃśuka flowers.
Because of the smoke, it was impossible to go from house to house. / Burned by the fire of Hara's wrath, crying out, intensely miserable,
ignited in every direction, the city of Tripura was consumed. / Palace spires shattered by the thousands.
Aerial cars, wonderfully inlaid with diverse jewels of many kinds, / and charming houses were burned by the blazing fire.
Torment reigned in groves of trees and likewise in inhabited quarters; / in all the shrines of the gods, flames flared and blazed.
Touched by the fire, they sank down and cried out in diverse voices; / heaps of charcoal, resembling mountain peaks, were seen there.
They praised the Lord of gods: “Save me, O Lord!” / Embracing one another, tortured by the fire,
the Dānavas were burned there by the hundreds, then by the thousands. / Lotus ponds covered with haṃsas and kāraṇḍava ducks, along with lotuses,
were scorched, burned by fire, as were the city's gardens and elongated pools / covered with unfading lotuses, extending for hundreds of yojanas.
Resembling mountain crests, palaces there adorned with jewels / fell, scorched by fire, like waterless clouds.
Together with women, children, and the elderly, upon cows, birds, and horses, / the merciless fire burned, driven by Hara's anger.
Those asleep with their wives, and many people sound asleep, / clinging tightly to a son, were burned by the enemy of Tripura.
Then, in that blazing city, women who were like Apsarases, / struck by the flames of fire, fell to the ground.
A certain wide-eyed young girl, adorned with strings of pearls, / bewildered by smoke and awakened, tormented by the flames,
thinking of her son, fell upon the surface of the earth. / Another woman of golden complexion, adorned with sapphires,
bewildered by the smoke, fell upon the surface of the earth. / Another, taking her friend by the hand, burns with her children.
Another of divine form, having seen this, bewildered by passion, / folded her hands at her head and petitioned the fire:
“If you desire enmity against the men who have offended, / what have women done wrong—we who are cuckoos in the cages of our homes?
O wicked, merciless, shameless one, what anger is this toward women? / You have no courtesy, no shame, no truth, devoid of purity!
Endowed with many forms and colors, perceptible—tell me: / have you not heard that all women in the world are unslayable?
Are these indeed your virtues, O burner, toward afflicting women— / no compassion, or mercy, or courtesy toward a woman?
Even barbarians show mercy upon seeing women, O fire! / You are worse than barbarians, hard to restrain, unfeeling!
Are these your qualities for burning and destruction? / Why do you bring down women, even those whose conduct is wicked?
O corrupt, pitiless, shameless fire of ill fortune, / you are hopeless, of vile conduct, mercilessly burning children!”
While they were lamenting thus, talking in many tones, / others, enraged and bewildered by grief for their children, cried aloud.
The merciless fire burned, furious like an enemy of all; / there was flame in the water of the lotus pool and even in the wells.
“Burning us, O barbarian, what state will you attain?” / To them lamenting thus, the fire spoke this word:
Vaiśvānara said: / “Not by my own will do I bring about your destruction; / I merely carry out the order, I am not the one who can bestow grace.
Overcome by anger here, I wander at will.” / Then Bāṇa of great splendor, seeing Tripura engulfed in flames,
seated upon his seat, spoke thus: “I have been destroyed by the gods, / who are of little substance and vile conduct, having complained to the Lord.
Without examining [the matter], I was burned by high-souled Śaṅkara; / no other enemy could slay me except Maheśvara.”
Having arisen, bearing upon his head the liṅga, Lord of the three worlds, / he went out from the city gate, leaving behind his kin himself,
and diverse jewels, and varied women. / Taking the liṅga upon his head, placed in the center of the city,
he praised the Lord of the lords of gods, Śiva, the master of the three worlds: / “O Hara, I have been consumed by you; if I am to be slain by you, O Śaṅkara,
by your grace, O Mahādeva, let not my liṅga perish! / For it has always been worshipped, O Mahādeva, with supreme devotion.
Even if I am to be slain by you, let not my liṅga perish! / This grasping of your feet is what must be attained by me, O Mahādeva.
In birth after birth, O Mahādeva, I am devoted to your feet!” / Having praised the God, the Supreme Lord, in the toṭaka meter:

“Om, obeisance to Śiva, Śaṅkara, the maker of all! Obeisance to the Auspicious One, the fierce Maheśa, source of existence! / O destroyer of the body of the flower-weaponed [Kāma], ender of Tripura, crusher of Andhaka!

Beloved of women, differentiated by desire, obeisance, obeisance, revered by the hosts of gods and Siddhas! / By hosts with faces of horses, monkeys, lions, and lordly elephants, and with exceedingly short and very long faces!

Incapable of being attained by Asuras, not afflicted by hundreds of diverse bodies, / bowed down to by the intensely devoted, O God bearing the crescent of the trembling moon, obeisance, O Blessed One!
Together with sons, wives, groups [of kin], and riches, give always victory and remembrance! / I am afflicted by hundreds of multiple bodies; today the course to the great hell has been reached.
Since the path of my sin does not turn back, it abandons even pure and undefiled actions; / compassion wanders, wanders bewildered in every direction; this bewilderment restrains evil thought.”
Whoever, restrained and pure in mind, should recite this divine toṭaka hymn, / Rudra will become a boon-giver to him, just as he was to Bāṇa.
Having heard this most divine hymn of praise, the god Maheśvara / was pleased with him at that time, the divine Maheśvara himself.
The Lord said: / “You need not fear, my child! Remain in Sauvarṇa, O Dānava, / together with sons, grandsons, wives, dependants, and servants.
From this day forth, O Bāṇa, you cannot be slain even by the gods!” / Furthermore, a boon was granted to him by the God of gods, O Pāṇḍava.
Imperishable and unfailing, he roamed fearlessly in the world. / Then Rudra restrained the seven-crested [fire].
Its third [city] was protected by the great-souled Śaṅkara; / it wanders constantly in the sky through the power of Rudra's splendor.
Thus Tripura was burned by the great-souled Śaṅkara, / and, blazed with garlands of flames, fell down upon the surface of the earth.
One [city] of his was brought down upon Śrīśaila, the destroyer of Tripura; / the second was brought down there upon Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
When Tripura was burned, O king, a crore of Rudras were established there; / it was brought down blazing there, therefore it is known as Jvāleśvara.
Rising upwards, its divine flame went to heaven; / then an outcry arose, encompassing the gods, asuras, and kiṃnaras.
Rudra immobilized that arrow in the excellent city of the Great Lord; / whoever goes thus to that Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
Having well enjoyed the fourteen worlds, O son of Pāṇḍu, / for a thousand crores of years, and another thirty crores,
Then, having reached the surface of the earth, he becomes a righteous king; / he enjoys the earth under a single umbrella—of this there is no doubt.
Holy from every side is this Amarakaṇṭaka, O great king; / he who goes to Amarakaṇṭaka during eclipses of the moon and sun,
The wise declare [the fruit] to be tenfold that of a horse sacrifice; / having seen the Great Lord there, he attains the heavenly world.
When the sun is seized by Rāhu, [the merits of Saṃnihitā] will gather; / all that very same merit [is attained] on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
A person obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice; / there, on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, is the place named Jvāleśvara.
Having bathed there, they go to heaven; those who die there do not return to rebirth; / whoever abandons his life's breaths at Jvāleśvara, O great king,
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, even with devotion—hear its fruit! / On Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, they become gods among immortals.
He attains the world of Rudra until the dissolution of all beings; / at the water on the slope of the mountain of the Lord of Immortals,
Foremost sages of good vows, by the crores, perform ascetic penance; / O king, the sacred domain of Amarakaṇṭaka extends for a yojana all around.
Whether free of desire or possessing desire, having bathed in the auspicious water of the Narmadā, / one is freed from sins and goes to the world of Rudra.

3.16.m: The sage said: / Those great souls, all the prominent men headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, / and the sages rich in ascetic penance, questioned Nārada:
“Declare the truth, O blessed one, regarding the great confluence of the Kāverī, / for the welfare of the worlds and for our own prosperity.
How are men who are ever devoted to sin and commit evil deeds / freed from all sins and go to the supreme abode? / This I wish to know, O blessed one; you ought to tell it.”
Nārada said: / “Listen all together, led by Yudhiṣṭhira: / Having performed a great sacrifice here, Kubera of true valor, / having reached this sacred ford, became greater than an empire.
He achieved accomplishment, O great king; hear that as I declare it: / Where the Kāverī meets the world-renowned Narmadā,
Having bathed there and become purified, Kubera of true valor, / the lord of yakṣas, performed ascetic penance for a great divine hundred years.
Pleased with him, Mahādeva granted an excellent boon: / ‘Hail, O yakṣa of great strength! Choose a boon as you desire; / state whatever purpose you wish, or whatever is in your mind.’
Kubera said: / ‘If you are pleased, O lord of gods, and if a boon is to be given to me, / may I be the original creator and ruler of all the yakṣas.’
Hearing the words of Kubera, the god Maheśvara was pleased; / having said ‘So be it,’ he disappeared right there.
Having obtained the boon, that yakṣa swiftly went to the yakṣa race; / honored by all the yakṣa lords, he was consecrated as king.
There is the confluence of the Kāverī, destroying all sins; / the men who do not know of it are cheated—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, a person should bathe there, / where there are the most sacred Kāverī and the great river Narmadā.
Having bathed there, O lord of kings, one should worship the bull-bannered god; / having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, he is honored in the world of Rudra.
He who enters fire, or he who undertakes fasting unto death, / his path is one of no return, just as Śaṅkara told me.
Attended by excellent women, he rejoices in heaven like Rudra / for sixty thousand years, and another sixty crores.
Abiding in the world of Rudra, he rejoices wherever he goes; / when his merit is exhausted and he falls, he becomes a righteous king,
Endowed with enjoyments, virtuous in nature, and born of an exalted family; / having properly drunk the water there, one obtains the fruit of a cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Those mortals who drink the auspicious water go to heaven; / the fruit which human beings attain between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā,
Having bathed at the confluence of the Kāverī, that same fruit arises for him; / thus, O lord of kings, the great confluence of the Kāverī, / known as Patreśvara, is the supreme remover of all sins.”

3.17.m: Nārada said: / “On the northern bank of the Narmadā is a sacred ford one yojana in extent, / known as Patreśvara, the supreme remover of all sins.
Having bathed there, a man rejoices with the gods, O king; / assuming forms at will, he sports for five thousand years.
Then one should go to Garjana, where the cloud appeared; / the name Indrajit was attained through the power of that sacred ford.
Then one should go to Megharāva, where the roaring of the cloud occurred; / there the attendant Meghanāda attained perfection of boons.
Then one should go, O lord of kings, to the place remembered as Brahmāvarta; / Brahmā is constantly present there, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having bathed there, O lord of kings, one is honored in the world of Brahmā; / then at the sacred ford Aṅgāreśvara, restrained and eating restricted food,
With his self cleansed of all sins, he goes to the world of Rudra; / then one should go, O lord of kings, to the excellent Kapilātīrtha.
Having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow; / then one should go to Kāñcītīrtha, frequented by hosts of divine sages.
Having bathed there, O king, a man attains Goloka; / then one should go, O lord of kings, to the excellent Kuṇḍaleśvara.
Present there, Rudra resides along with Umā; / having bathed there, O lord of kings, he becomes invincible even to the gods.
Then one should go to Pippaleśvara, which destroys all sins; / having gone there, O lord of kings, he is honored in the world of Rudra.
Then one should go, O lord of kings, to pure Vimaleśvara; / there the lovely crest of the gods was brought down by the Lord.
Giving up one's life's breaths there, one would attain the world of Rudra; / then one should go to Puṣkariṇī and perform a bath there.
Merely by bathing there, a man obtains half the seat of Indra; / the Narmadā, best of rivers, emerged from the body of Rudra.
It delivers all beings, both motionless and moving; / by the supreme God of all gods, the great-souled Lord,
It was declared to the assemblies of sages, and particularly to us; / indeed, this excellent river Narmadā is praised by the munis.
She came forth from Rudra's body desiring the welfare of the worlds, / always removing all sins, bowed to by all living beings,

and praised by gods, gandharvas, and apsarases:
'Homage to you whose waters are holy, O primeval one! Homage to you who flow to the sea!

Homage to you, [praised] by hosts of sages, who issued from Śaṅkara's body!
Homage to you, O fair-faced one enveloped in dharma! Homage to you, praised by the hosts of gods alone!

Homage to you who purify all pure things! Homage to you, worshipped in all the worlds!'
And whichever person recites this hymn constantly with a pure mind,

a brāhmaṇa attains the Veda, a kṣatriya becomes victorious,
a vaiśya gains profit, and a śūdra attains a good realm.

3.18.m:
Nārada said:
From that time forward, Brahmā and the other sages rich in asceticism
attend upon the Narmadā, O king, free from desire and anger.

Seeing that trident of the god fallen to the surface of the earth,
its merit was proclaimed by the great-souled Śaṅkara:

"The great holy place renowned as Śūlabheda is most meritorious;
having bathed there and worshipped the god, one gains the fruit of [gifting] a thousand cows.

Whoever, O ruler of men, spends three nights at that holy place
and worships Mahādeva, for him there is no rebirth.

Then one should go to Bhīmeśvara, and to the excellent Narmadeśvara,
to the most holy Ādityeśvara, together with ghee and honey.

Having worshipped Mallikeśvara, the fruit of one's birth is complete.
Then one should behold Varuṇeśvara, and the excellent Nīrājeśvara;

from beholding the five shrines, one receives the fruit of all holy places.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to where the battle was won;

renowned as Koṭitīrtha, where the asuras were fought,
where those dānavas, arrogant with strength, were slain, O king.

Their heads were taken; having assembled, they were slain.
By them the god was installed, the trident-handed Maheśvara.

Ten million were slain there, hence it is known as Koṭīśvara.
From the sight of that holy place, one goes to heaven with one's body.

Then Indra, out of pettiness, bound it with a thunderbolt stake;
from that time forward, humans' going to heaven [in bodily form] was prevented.

When dead, he attains the state of Rudra, and is not born here again;
having gone to heaven and then ruled, having departed, then [he goes] to the celestial world.

Having worshipped Mahādeva in this way on the thirteenth day,
a man, merely by bathing there, obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.

Then, O king of kings, one should go to the most splendid holy place,
the excellent Agastyeśvara, for the destruction of men's sins.

Having bathed there, O king, a person is freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika,

concentrated and with senses conquered, one should bathe the god with ghee;
united with twenty-one generations of his family, he is not parted from the realm of the Lord.

One should give cows, shoes, an umbrella, and a blanket,
and food for brāhmaṇas; all becomes multiplied ten million fold.

Then, O king of kings, one should go to the matchless Ravistava;
having bathed there, O king, a person attains a throne.

On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the renowned holy place of Śakra;
having fasted for one night, one should perform a bath there.

Having bathed according to proper rule, one should worship Janārdana;
one gains the fruit of a thousand cows and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

Then one should go to Ṛṣitīrtha, which takes away all sins of men;
merely by bathing there, a person is honored in the world of Śiva.

And right there is the most splendid holy place of Nārada;
merely by bathing there, a person gains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Then one should go to Devatīrtha, created by Brahmā in ancient times;
having bathed there, O king, a person is honored in the world of Brahmā.

Then one should go to Amarakaṇṭaka, established by the immortals in ancient times;
merely by bathing there, a person gains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Then, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Vāmaneśvara;
having seen Vāmana there, one is freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa.

Then a man should certainly go to Ṛṣitīrtha and to Īśāneśa;
then, having seen Vaṭeśvara, the fruit of his birth is complete.

Then one should go to Bhīmeśvara, which destroys all illnesses;
merely by bathing, O king, a person is freed from all suffering.

Then, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Vāraṇeśvara;
having bathed there, O king, a person is freed from all suffering.

Then one should go to Somatīrtha and behold the supreme Moon;
having bathed there, O king, endowed with supreme devotion,

at that moment, residing in a divine body, he rejoices like Śiva for a long time;
for sixty thousand years he is honored in the world of Śiva.

Then, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Piṅgaleśvara;
by fasting for a day and a night, one obtains the fruit of three nights.

Whoever gives a tawny cow at that holy place, O king of kings,
as many hairs as there are on her and on the herd born of her,

for so many thousands of years he is honored in the world of Rudra.
Whoever relinquishes his life-breaths there, O ruler of men,

rejoices for imperishable time, as long as the moon and sun endure.
Those humans who dwell relying upon the bank of the Narmadā,

when dead, go to heaven, just as the virtuous do.
One should go to Surabhikeśvara, to the hellish Koṭikeśvara;

at the Descent of the Gaṅgā, that day is holy, there is no doubt.
Then one should go to Nandītīrtha and perform a bath there;

Nandīśa is pleased with him, and he is honored in the world of Soma.
Then one should go to Dvīpeśvara, to Vyāsatīrtha, an ascetic grove.

In ancient times, the great river, frightened of Vyāsa, was turned back there;
roared at with 'Huṃ' by Vyāsa, she then went to the south.

Whoever performs circumambulation at that holy place, O ruler of men,
Vyāsa becomes pleased with him, and he attains his desired fruit.

Whoever wraps the radiant god with an altar with a thread,
sports for imperishable time, just like Rudra himself.

Then, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Eraṇḍītīrtha;
having bathed at the confluence, a person is freed from all sins.

Eraṇḍī is renowned in the three worlds as destroying sin.
Alternatively, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina,
becoming pure, a person, having bathed, devoted to fasting,

should feed a single brāhmaṇa, and ten million are [as good as] fed.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī, delighted with devotional disposition,

placing a pearl oyster shell on one's head and plunging into the water
mingled with the water of the Narmadā, one is freed from all offenses.

Whoever performs circumambulation at that holy place, O ruler of men,
by him the earth of seven continents has been circumambulated.

Then, having bathed at Suvarṇatilaka and given gold,
he is honored in the world of Rudra by means of a golden celestial chariot.
Then, having fallen from heaven in course of time, he becomes a mighty king. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the confluence of the Ikṣu river,
which is renowned in the three worlds and divine; Śiva is present there. / Having bathed there, O king, a man attains leadership among the Gaṇas.
Then one should go to Skaṃdatīrtha, which destroys all sins; / merely by bathing, it removes sin committed since birth.
Then one should go to Āṃgirasa and perform a bath there; / his fruit is that of a thousand cows, and he is honoured in Rudra's world.
Then one should go to Lāṃgalatīrtha, which destroys all sins; / having gone there, O king of kings, one should perform a bath there.
He is freed from sins committed in seven births; there is no doubt of this. / Then one should go to Vaṭeśvara, the highest of all tīrthas.
Having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. / Then one should go to Saṃgameśvara, the supreme remover of all sins.
Having bathed there, a man obtains kingship; there is no doubt of this. / Having approached Bhadratīrtha, whatever man gives a gift—
by the power of that tīrtha, everything becomes multiplied ten-millionfold. / If any woman should perform a bath there,
she becomes equal to Gaurī and goes to Indra; there is no doubt. / Then one should go to Aṅgāreśvara and perform a bath there.
Merely by bathing there, a man is honoured in Rudra's world. / One should perform a bath there on the Aṅgārakī fourth day.
Having Murāri's command fulfilled, he rejoices for an imperishable time. / Having bathed at Ayonisaṃgama, one would not see the abode of the womb.
Having gone to Pāṇḍaveśvara, one should perform a bath there; / invulnerable to gods and asuras, he rejoices for an imperishable time.
Then, having gone to Viṣṇu's world, endowed with play and pleasures, / and having enjoyed great pleasures there, he is born as a king among mortals.
One should go to Kaṃbotikeśvara and perform a bath there; / when the sun's northern course has arrived, whatever he might wish becomes his.
Then one should go to Candrabhāgā and perform a bath there; / merely by bathing there, a man is honoured in Soma's world.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the renowned tīrtha of Śakra, / worshipped by the king of gods and bowed to even by the gods.
Having bathed there, O king, and given a gift of gold, / or whoever releases a bull that has the lustre of a dark blue colour—
as many hairs as there are on the bull and in its line of offspring, / for that many thousands of years a man dwells in Hara's city.
Then, fallen from heaven, he becomes a mighty king; / over thousands of white horses, O ruler of men,
he becomes the master among mortals, by the power of that tīrtha. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to Brahmāvarta, which has no superior.
Having bathed there, O king, a man should offer libations to the ancestors and gods. / Having fasted for one night and offered a funeral ball according to rule,
as when the sun is in Virgo, what is accumulated becomes imperishable. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Kapilātīrtha.
Having bathed there, O king, whoever gives a brown cow / obtains that fruit which is gained by giving the entire earth.
Narmadeśvara is a supreme tīrtha; there never was nor will there ever be [its equal]. / Having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
A king who goes everywhere on the earth is born from there, / endowed with all auspicious marks, completely free from all diseases.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful tīrtha, / a delightful sanctuary of Āditya, consecrated by the Lord.
Having bathed there, O king of kings, and given a gift according to one's means, / by the power of that tīrtha, what is given becomes imperishable.
Those who are poor, those who are diseased, and those who have performed evil deeds / are freed from all sins and proceed to the world of Sūrya.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, / whoever dwells in the sanctuary, selfless and with senses restrained,
is not born diseased, nor blind, nor deaf at that time; / fortunate and endowed with handsome form, he becomes dear to women.
This greatly holy tīrtha was spoken of by Mārkaṇḍeya; / those who go away [without visiting], O king of kings, are deceived, no doubt.
Then one should go to Māseśvara and perform a bath there; / merely by bathing there, a man attains heaven.
Dwelling in all the worlds, he rejoices as long as fourteen Indras [endure]. / Having stayed near there, [one should go to] the penance grove Nāgeśvara.
Having bathed there, O king of kings, becoming pure and concentrated, / he sports with many serpent maidens for an imperishable time.
One should go to Kubera's abode, where Kubera resides; / Kāleśvara is a supreme tīrtha where Kubera was gratified,
where, having bathed, O king of kings, one obtains all prosperity. / Then towards the west one should go to the excellent abode of the Maruts.
Having bathed there, O king of kings, becoming pure and concentrated, / the wise man should then give gold and food according to his ability.
By means of the Puṣpaka aerial car, he goes to the world of Vāyu. / Then one should go to Mamatīrtha in the month of Māgha, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform a bath there; / one should then take a night meal; he will not enter the narrow passage of the womb.
Then one should go to Ahalyātīrtha and perform a bath there; / merely by bathing there, a man rejoices with apsarases.
Having performed austerities at Pārameśvara, Ahalyā attained liberation. / When the month of Caitra has arrived, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight,
on that day of Kāmadeva, one should worship Ahalyā; / wherever a man is born, he becomes beloved there,
dear to women, prosperous, like a second Kāmadeva. / Having approached Ayodhyā, the renowned tīrtha of Śakra,
merely by bathing there, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. / Then one should go to Somatīrtha and merely perform a bath.
Merely by bathing there, a man is completely freed from all sins; / during a lunar eclipse, O king of kings, it brings about the destruction of sin.
Somatīrtha is renowned in the three worlds, O king, and bears great fruit; / and whoever performs the cāndrāyaṇa penance at that tīrtha, O ruler of men,
with soul purified of all sins, he goes to Soma's world. / By entering fire, or in water, or indeed through fasting,
he who dies at Somatīrtha is not born again among mortals. / Then one should go to Stambhatīrtha and perform a bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man is honoured in Soma's world. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the unsurpassed Viṣṇutīrtha,
the unsurpassed Viṣṇutīrtha, famous as Yodhanīpura, / where asuras were fought in tens of millions by Vāsudeva.
A tīrtha arose there; Viṣṇu becomes pleased here. / By fasting for a day and night, one removes the murder of a brahmin.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Tāpaseśvara, / known as Amohaka, where one should offer libations to the ancestors.
On the full moon or on the new moon, one should perform a śrāddha according to rule. / Having bathed there, O king, a man should offer a funeral ball to the ancestors.
There are rocks shaped like elephants situated in the middle of the water; / on that one should offer a funeral ball, especially in the month of Vaiśākha.
The ancestors are gratified for as long as the earth endures. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to unequalled Siddheśvara;
having gone there, O king of kings, one should approach Gaṇapati. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the liṅga where Janārdana is;
bathing there, O king of kings, one is glorified in Viṣṇu's realm. / On the southern bank of the Narmadā there is a most beautiful sacred ford;
there Kāmadeva himself, that great one, performed ascetic heat: / for a thousand divine years he attended upon Śaṅkara.
Though burned by the great-souled Śaṅkara during the change of his deep meditation, / [and like] fire upon the white phase of the moon, resembling a white knot,
all those [parts of him] that were burned stood established as Kusumeśvara. / Through the thousand divine years, Maheśvara became pleased with them;
Rudra, accompanied by Umā, was pleased with them and granted a boon, / having completely liberated all of them stationed on the bank of the Narmadā.
By the power of that sacred ford, he attained godhood once again. / [Kāma said:] 'By your grace, O Mahādeva, may this sacred ford become supreme,'
extending half a yojana all around in the directions. / A man who bathes in that sacred ford, intent upon fasting,
in the form of the flower-weaponed [god] is glorified in Rudra's realm. / By Vaiśvānara, by Yama, by Kāmadeva, and by Vāyu,
ascetic heat was performed, O king of kings, having gone right there in ancient times. / Near the Andhona, and indeed not very far from it,
bathing, giving, eating, and the offering of rice-balls [should be done] right there, / or entering fire, into water, or through fasting to death;
there is no return for one who dies even within half a yojana. / The best of men should bathe [the deity] with the water of the Traiyambaka;
and having offered the rice-ball according to rule at the root of the Andhona, / his ancestors are gratified as long as the sun and moon [endure].
When the northern course of the sun has arrived, whoever bathes there— / whether a man or a woman—pure, should dwell in the sacred precinct.
From the worship of the god Siddheśvara at dawn, a man / attains the goal of the virtuous, which cannot be attained by all great sacrifices.
And when, at the time of the sacred ford, he becomes handsome and fortunate, / he becomes a king among mortals over the range bounded by the ocean.
One who does not see the guardian of the field, the very mighty guardian with the staff, / his pilgrimage becomes useless without seeing Karṇakuṇḍala.
Knowing the fruit of this sacred ford, all the gods gathered, / released a shower of flowers, and praised Kusumeśvara.

3.19.m: Nārada said: / Then one should go with devotion to Bhārgaveśa, where by Viṣṇu / the Dānavas, roared at by the god, went to dissolution.
Bathing there, O king of kings, one is released from all sins. / Hear also the origin of Śuklatīrtha, O joy of the Pāṇḍus.
On the delightful peak of the Himālaya, adorned with various minerals, / resembling the rising sun, like molten gold,
with stairways of diamond and crystal, with a stone floor of variegated slabs, / divine, made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with various lotuses—
there Mārkaṇḍa questioned Mahādeva, who was seated there, the omniscient, imperishable Lord, / who favors the worlds, peaceful, surrounded by hosts of attendants,
with the attendants headed by Skanda, Nandin, Mahākāla, and Vīrabhadra, / the god accompanied by Umā:
[Mārkaṇḍa said:] 'O God of gods, O Mahādeva, praised by Indra, Kāma, and others! / Terrified of worldly existence, tell me the easy means,
O Blessed One, Lord of past and future, destroyer of all sins: / tell me, O Maheśvara, the supreme sacred ford of all sacred fords.'
The Lord said: / 'Listen, O highly fortunate brahmin, skilled in all scriptures; / surrounded by the assembly of sages, go and perform your bathing and other rites.
Manu, Atri, Yājñavalkya, Kaśyapa, and Aṅgiras, / Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati,
Nārada, and Gautama, desiring righteousness, ask: / "The Gaṅgā at Kanakhala is meritorious, as are Prayāga, Puṣkara, and Gayā,
and Kurukṣetra is meritorious when the sun is seized by Rāhu; / whether by day or by night, Śuklatīrtha yields great fruit.
From seeing it, from touching it, and from bathing, meditation, and acquiring ascetic power, / and from fire offerings and fasting, the fruit of Śuklatīrtha is great.
Śuklatīrtha, exceedingly meritorious, is situated upon the river; / the royal sage named Cāṇikya attained accomplishment there.
This sacred site arose, situated over the span of a yojana; / Śuklatīrtha is exceedingly meritorious, destroying all sins.
When the top of the tree is seen, it removes the sin of killing a brahmin. / Here, O best of sages, I abide with Umā.
In the spotless month of Vaiśākha, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, / coming forth from Kailāsa, I am present right there.
Gods, Kinnaras, and Gandharvas, likewise Siddhas and Vidyādharas, / attendants, Apsarases, and Nāgas—all the gods assemble,
and staying in the sky, they stand in aerial chariots that fulfill every desire; / and they come to Śuklatīrtha, O king of kings, desiring righteousness.
Just as a cloth is made white by a washerman with water, / in Śuklatīrtha the sin accumulated since birth is cast off.
Bathing and giving are exceedingly meritorious, O Mārkaṇḍa, best of sages; / there has been no sacred ford greater than Śuklatīrtha, nor will there ever be.
Having committed evil deeds in early life, a man / casts them off in Śuklatīrtha by fasting for a day and a night.
By austerity, celibate studenthood, sacrifices, or giving again— / the nourishment that comes from a gift to the gods does not come even from a hundred sacrifices.
And on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, / having fasted, one should bathe the supreme Lord, the god, with clarified butter.
Accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, he will not fall from the state of the Lord. / Śuklatīrtha is the supreme sacred ford, frequented by sages and Siddhas;
bathing there, O king, there is no rebirth. / Having bathed at Śuklatīrtha, one should worship the bull-bannered god;
one should keep a night vigil there with auspicious things such as dance and song; / and at dawn at Śuklatīrtha, one should perform bathing and worship of the deity.
Afterward, devoted to the vow of Śiva, pure, one should feed the preceptor; / and one should provide food according to one's ability, without stinginess in wealth.
Then, having circumambulated [him], one should slowly approach the presence of the god. / Whoever does this, hear the meritorious fruit of him:
mounted upon a celestial aerial car, praised by hosts of Apsarases, / endowed with strength equal to Śiva, he abides until the deluge of creatures.
Whatever woman gives auspicious gold at Śuklatīrtha, / bathes the god with clarified butter, and reveres Kumāra,
whoever acts thus with devotion—hear the meritorious fruit of her: / she rejoices, dwelling in the world of the gods as long as the fourteen Indras [rule].
Or on the solstice, on the fourteenth day, at the sun's passage into a zodiac sign, or likewise at the equinox, / having bathed while fasting, self-controlled, composed,
one should give gifts according to one's ability so that Hari and Śaṅkara may be pleased; / by the power of Śuklatīrtha, everything becomes inexhaustible.
Whoever gives away in marriage at the sacred ford [the daughter of] a brahmin who is helpless and destitute, or even one who has a protector—hear the meritorious fruit of him:
as many hairs as there are on him and in the families born from him, / for so many thousands of years is he glorified in Śiva's realm.'

3.20.m:
Nārada said:
Then one should go to Naraka and perform an ablution there. / Merely upon bathing there, a man does not see hell.
Hear the glorification of this pilgrimage place, O delight of Pāṇḍu: / In that pilgrimage place, O king of kings, whatever bones one casts,
They all dissolve, and the man is born endowed with beauty. / Then one should go to Gotīrtha; having seen it, one is freed from sin.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Kapilātīrtha. / Having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Especially when the month of Jyeṣṭha arrives, on the fourteenth day: / Having fasted there, the man who devotedly gives a Kapila cow,
Lighting a lamp with ghee, should bathe Śiva with ghee; / Having offered a bilva fruit with ghee, and then performed circumambulation,
Whoever gives a Kapila cow adorned with bells / Becomes equal to Śiva and is not born here again.
Especially when Tuesday arrives on the fourth day, / Having bathed Śiva with devotion, feeding the brāhmaṇas,
And likewise on Tuesday's ninth day, as well as on the new moon day, / One should diligently bathe [him] there; he will become handsome and fortunate.
One should bathe the liṅga with ghee and worship the twice-born with devotion. / In the Puṣpaka aerial chariot, surrounded by thousands,
He attains the realm of Śiva, and no misfortune will befall him there; / He rejoices for imperishable time, just like Rudra himself.
And when, through the consequence of his deeds, he comes to the mortal world, / He becomes a righteous king, born handsome and mighty.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the unsurpassed Ṛṣitīrtha. / A sage named Tṛṇabindu had stayed there, burnt by a curse;
By the power of that pilgrimage place, the twice-born was released from sin. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the unsurpassed Gaṇeśvara.
When the month of Śrāvaṇa arrives, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, / Merely upon bathing there, a man is exalted in the realm of Rudra.
Having offered water libations to the ancestors, he is freed from the three debts. / Near Gaṇeśvara is the excellent Gaṅgāvadana.
Whether without desire or with desire, a human who bathes there / Is freed from sins accrued from birth—of this there is no doubt.
One should always perform an ablution there on festive days; / Having offered water libations to the ancestors, he is freed from the three debts.
Whatever fruit was perceived at Prayāga by the great-souled Śaṅkara, / That very same entire religious merit exists at the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Rāhu, and the Sun.
In the western place nearby, not very far from it, / Is the place called Daśāśvamedhika, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having fasted for one night, in the month of Bhādrapada, / A man, having bathed on the new moon, goes to where Śaṅkara is.
One should always perform an ablution there on festive days; / Having offered water libations to the ancestors, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
To the west of Daśāśvamedha, Bhṛgu, the best of brāhmaṇas, / Served the Lord for a divine thousand years.
He stood covered by an anthill, with his dwelling to the south. / And great astonishment arose in Umā and Śaṅkara.
Gaurī asked the god: 'Who is this staying here? / A god, or else a demon? Tell me, O Maheśvara!'

The Lord said:
'Named Bhṛgu, he is the best among the twice-born, an eminent sage among ṛṣis. / Established in absorption, he meditates on me and asks for a boon, O dear one.'

Laughing at that, the goddess spoke in reply to the Lord: / 'A mass of swirling smoke has arisen, yet even today you are not pleased. / He has found you difficult to propitiate; there is no deliberation needed here.'

The god said:
'You do not know, O great goddess: he is agitated by anger. / I will show it as it truly is, and I will do what pleases you.'
The bull, who is dharma personified, was then remembered by the god of gods. / Just from the recollection of the god of gods, the bull promptly appeared.
He spoke in human speech: 'Let your command be given, O Lord!' / 'The brāhmaṇa is covered by anthills; cast him down onto the ground.'
Stationed in yoga and meditating, he was then struck down by him. / Burning with anger that very moment, he raised his hand against the bull.
Calling out thus: 'Where are you going, O bull? / Today I shall slay you visibly, you sinful bull!'
Having thus been assaulted, the brāhmaṇa then saw the bull ascend into the sky; / He looked again into the heavens—this most excellent wonder!
Then, as Rudra laughed, the sage stood before him. / Seeing the third eye, he fell to the ground in embarrassment.

Bowing like a staff upon the ground, he praised the supreme Lord: / 'Bowing before the lord of beings, the source of existence, who possess a divine form, / I, terrified of worldly existence, O Lord of the world, submit a true matter:
What human is able to speak the multitude of your qualities, O Lord? / Perhaps Vāsuki, whose faces number a thousand!
Out of devotion to you, O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the world, I am garrulous in your praise; / O adorable one, forgive this being! Be gracious to me, who have fallen at your feet!
You are sattva, rajas, and tamas in preservation, creation, and destruction, O God! / Apart from you, O Lord of the world, O sovereign of the world, there is no deity whatsoever.
Through restraints, observances, sacrifices, gifts, the study of the Vedas, and the exertion of contemplation— / All this is not worth a thousandth part of devotion to you.
Whether the attainment of superior elixirs, chemical arts, the magic sword, magical eye-salve, magic slippers, or the like, / The marks of those bowed down to you are visibly seen in this birth.
Even if one bows deceitfully, you give dharma to those who desire it, O God. / Devotion which severs worldly existence has been fashioned for liberation, O Lord.
Addicted to another's wife and another's wealth, afflicted by insult, another's sorrow, and grief, / Dedicated to watching another's face—protect me, O supreme Lord!
Burnt by false pride, sporting in momentary and transient splendour, O God, / Cruel, inclined to the wrong path, fallen—save me, O Lord of gods!
Expectation has been filled only by miserable sensory faculties and relatives; / Yet it is worthless, O Śaṅkara; why do you mock me, a fool?
Take away thirst quickly! Give me the fortune that resides eternally in the heart! / Cut the bonds of pride and delusion! Deliver me across, O Mahādeva!'
This divine hymn named 'The Dawn of Compassion' bestows accomplishments; / Whosoever recites it full of devotion, with him Śiva becomes pleased, just as he was with Bhṛgu.

The Lord said:
'I am pleased with you, O brāhmaṇa; ask for the desired boon.' / Accompanied by Umā, the god indeed granted him the boon.

Bhṛgu said:
'If you are pleased, O Lord of gods, if a boon is to be given to me: / May this become a Rudravedī; grant this to me!'

The Lord said:
'So be it, O chief among the twice-born! It will be a place of anger: / Even between a father and son, there will not be agreement.'
From that time forward, all the gods headed by Brahmā, along with the kinnaras, / Revere the pilgrimage place of Bhṛgu, where Maheśvara was pleased.
From seeing that pilgrimage place, one is instantly freed from sin. / Even helpless creatures, as well as those in control of themselves, who die there,
The destination of what is most secret of secrets would surely be theirs. / This vast sacred field destroys all sins;
having bathed there, they go to heaven; those who die there are free from rebirth. / Then shoes, an umbrella, food, and gold should be given,
and a meal according to one's capacity; for him that becomes inexhaustible. / Whoever should give a gift at an eclipse of the sun, even as he pleases,
or bathe in the sacred water, whatever the gift, for him it becomes inexhaustible. / During eclipses of the moon and sun, the unmatched release of a bull [should be performed];
foolish men do not know it, deluded by the illusion of Viṣṇu. / O king, situated on the Narmadā is the divine Vṛṣatīrtha.
A man who hears even once the glorification of Bhṛgutīrtha / is freed from all sins and goes to the realm of Rudra.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to excellent Gautameśvara. / Having bathed there, O king, devoted to fasting,
he is honored in the world of Brahmā in a golden aerial chariot. / Then one should go to Dhautapāpa, where indeed [sins] were washed by the bull;
it is situated on the Narmadā, O king, destroying all mortal sins. / A man having bathed at that sacred ford wipes away the killing of a brahmin.
O great king, whoever casts off his life at that sacred ford, / having four arms and three eyes, will possess power equal to Rudra.
Possessing valor equal to Rudra, he would dwell [there] for more than ten thousand kalpas; / and when a great time has passed, he would become the sole ruler of the earth.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Eraṇḍītīrtha. / The fruit that was observed at Prayāga, as spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya,
that fruit a human being obtains, O king, simply by bathing. / And in the month of Bhādrapada, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
having fasted for one night, one should perform a bath there; / he is not tormented by Yama’s messengers, and he goes to the realm of Indra.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to where Janārdana became perfected, / famed as Hiraṇyadvīpa, which destroys all sins.
A man having bathed there, O king, will become wealthy and handsome. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the great sacred ford Kanakhala.
Austerity was practiced at that sacred ford by Garuḍa, O ruler of men. / Celebrated in all the worlds, a yoginī abides there;
she sports with yogins and dances with Śiva. / A man having bathed there, O king, is honored in the realm of Rudra.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the unsurpassed Īśatīrtha; / freed there, the lord went upward without a doubt.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to where Janārdana became perfected, / assuming the form of the Boar, the inconceivable Supreme Lord.
A man having bathed at Varāhatīrtha, especially on the twelfth day, / reaches the realm of Viṣṇu and does not go to hell.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the unsurpassed Somatīrtha; / especially on the full moon day one should perform a bath there.
And having bowed down to Īśāna, Bali is pleased with him. / The divine city of Hariścandra is seen in the sky,
surrounded by discus-banners, with its dwelling adorned with serpents, / frequented by deer and water-animals through the surge of the Narmadā's waters.
And Viṣṇu spoke to Śaṅkara of dwelling in that place. / A man having bathed at Dvīpeśvara would obtain much gold.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to Rudrakanyā at the confluence; / merely upon bathing there, a man would attain the abode of the Goddess.
Then one should go to Devatīrtha, revered by all the gods. / Having bathed there, O king of kings, he rejoices with the deities.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the unsurpassed Śikhitīrtha; / whatever gift is given there is multiplied ten-millionfold.
In the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, one should perform a bath there. / If he feeds a single brahmin, ten million are fed.
At Bhṛgutīrtha, O king of kings, ten million sacred waters are situated. / Whether without desire or with desire, a human being should bathe there;
he obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and rejoices with the deities. / There Bhṛgu, the best of sages, attains perfection; / an incarnation was made by that noble Śaṅkara.

3.21.m: Nārada said: / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Vihageśvara; / by seeing it, O king of kings, one is freed from all sins.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Narmadeśvara; / having bathed there, O king, a man is honored in the heavenly world.
Then one should go to Aśvatīrtha and perform a bath there; / a man is born fortunate, handsome, and enjoying pleasures.
Then he should go to Pitāmaha, fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times; / bathing there with devotion, a man should offer a ball of rice to the ancestors.
He should offer water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass; / by the power of that sacred ford, everything becomes inexhaustible.
Having reached Sāvitrītīrtha, he who performs a bath, / shaking off all sins, is honored in the world of Brahmā.
And right there is the very beautiful ford Manoharā; / having bathed there, O king, a man is honored in the world of the ancestors.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Mānasatīrtha; / having bathed there, O king, a man is honored in the realm of Rudra.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the unsurpassed Kratutīrtha, / celebrated in all the worlds, destroying all sins.
Whatever desires he prays for—cattle, sons, and riches— / he would obtain all of them, O ruler of men, having bathed there.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the famed Tridaśadyoti; / there the daughters of ṛṣis of good vows perform austerity [praying]:
“May the Lord, the imperishable master, be the husband of us all.” / Pleased with them, Mahādeva, Hara bearing a fierce form,
with a distorted face and terrifying, approached that sacred ford; / there the Supreme Lord [became] the groom to the maidens, O great king.
And he who attends to the prosperity of maidens, gives the gift of a maiden; / the sacred ford there, O great king, is known as Daśakanya.
Having bathed there and worshiped the god, he is freed from all sins. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to what is celebrated as Svargabindu;
having bathed there, O king, a man does not see misfortune. / Then one should go to Apsareśa and perform a bath there;
dwelling in the world of nāgas, he sports and rejoices with apsarases. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Narakatīrtha;
having bathed there and worshiped the god, he does not go to hell. / Devoted to fasting, one should then go to Bhārabhūta;
having reached this sacred ford, an incarnation of Śambhu, / and having worshiped Virūpākṣa, he is honored in the realm of Rudra.
A man having bathed at that sacred ford Bhārabhūta of the noble one, / wherever he dies, his attainment is certainly that of the Gaṇas' realm.
Having worshiped Maheśvara during the month of Kārttika, / the wise say it is a hundred times more [meritorious] than a horse sacrifice.
Having prepared a hundred lamps filled with clarified butter, he should offer them; / he goes in aerial chariots resembling the sun to where Śaṅkara is.
Whoever gives a bull resembling a conch, the kunda flower, or the moon, / goes to the realm of Rudra in a vehicle yoked to bulls.
And whoever gives a single offering of boiled rice at that sacred ford, O ruler of men, / rice boiled in milk mixed with honey, and various kinds of eatables,
According to one's capacity, O best of kings, one should feed [Brahmins] together with dakṣiṇā; / by the power of that sacred bath, everything becomes multiplied ten-millionfold.
Sprinkling the water of the Narmadā and worshipping the bull-bannered [Śiva], / they do not see misfortune, on account of the power of that sacred bath.
Having reached this sacred bath, he who gives up his vital breaths, / with his soul purified of all sins, goes to where Śaṅkara dwells.
Whoever enters the water at that sacred bath, O lord of men, / goes to the realm of Rudra on a chariot harnessed with swans.
As long as the moon and the sun, the Himālaya and the great ocean endure, / as long as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā flow, for that long he is glorified in heaven.
He who undertakes fasting unto death at that sacred bath, O lord of men— / that man, O best of kings, is never born again into dwelling in a womb.
Then, O best of kings, one should go to the excellent Aṭavītīrtha; / having bathed there, O king, a man obtains half the seat of Indra.
Then one should go to Śṛṅgatīrtha, which destroys all sins; / merely by bathing there, indeed, the status of a follower of Gaṇeśa is assured.
And the confluence of the Eraṇḍī and Narmadā is renowned in the worlds; / there is a sacred bath of great merit, which destroys all sins.
Intent on fasting, always devoted to Brahman, / having bathed there, O best of kings, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Then, O best of kings, one should go to the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean, / known as Jamadagni, where Janārdana attained perfection,
where Indra, having sacrificed with numerous sacrifices, became the lord of the gods. / Having bathed there, O king, at the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean,
a man attains the fruit of three horse sacrifices, / union with the western ocean, and the opening of the gate to liberation.
There the gods together with the gandharvas, the sages, the siddhas and cāraṇas, / worship the lord of the gods, Vimaleśvara, at the three junctions of the day.
Purified in soul from all sins, he is glorified in the realm of Rudra; / there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred bath superior to Vimaleśvara.
Those who, having fasted there, behold Vimaleśvara, / purified in soul from all sins, go to the realm of Rudra.
Then, O best of kings, one should go to the excellent Keśinītīrtha; / having bathed there, O king, a man devoted to fasting,
having fasted for one night, restrained and temperate in food, / is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin by the power of that sacred bath.
And he who beholds Sāgareśvara, an ablution in all sacred waters— / Śiva stands residing within the whirlpool over the distance of a yojana.
Having seen him, all sacred baths are seen, no doubt; / completely freed from all sins, he goes to where Rudra dwells.
From the confluence of the Narmadā up to Amarakaṇṭaka, / between them, O great king, ten million sacred waters are situated in the water.
Wandering from sacred bath to sacred bath is a course of conduct frequented by ten million sages, / by those keeping the sacred fires, by divine beings, and by all devoted to spiritual knowledge.
They, frequented by these [sages], O best of kings, grant desired objects; / and whoever recites this daily, or listens with devotion,
all the sacred baths sprinkle him, O Pāṇḍava, / and the Narmadā is always pleased with him; of this there is no doubt.
Rudra and the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya become pleased with him; / a barren woman obtains sons, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate.
A husband obtains a young maiden, and whatever fruit one desires, / all that indeed one obtains; no doubt should be entertained here.
A Brahmin attains the Veda, a kṣatriya becomes victorious, / a vaiśya acquires grain, and a śūdra attains a good destiny.
A fool acquires knowledge. The man who recites it at the three junctions of the day / never sees hell, nor does he enter a base rebirth.

3.22.m: Nārada said: / Thus has been told to you, O king, the excellent sacred bath of the Narmadā. / Formerly, the terrible fear born of a curse upon the daughters of gandharvas
was destroyed, O great king, by the fire of a drop of Revā water; / through the touch of a drop of Revā water, a human being becomes liberated.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / O venerable one, how and whence was the curse incurred by the many maidens? / Whose offspring were they, what were their names, and what was their age?
How were they liberated through the touch of the waters of the Revā from the consequence arising from the curse? / Where did they bathe? Tell me all this, O lord.
The glorification of the Narmadā's sacred waters causes astonishment; / even from hearing it, the destruction of the stain of sins is spoken of.
By whomever the word 'Narmadā, Narmadā' is uttered, / his is eternal liberation for as long as the moon and stars endure.
The excellent glorification of the Revā has been spoken by you before; / nevertheless, O virtuous one, let this account be related.

Moreover, an excellent narrative is to be cherished by the wise. / Therefore I ask, O best of Brahmins, about the excellent glorification of the Revā; / tell, O lord, the legendary history, the radiant story of the maidens.
Nārada said: / Listen, O tiger among kings, to the supreme story pregnant with dharma, / as the fire-drill has fire within it, and dharma indeed comes from the creator of Brahman.
There was a gandharva named Śukasaṃgīti, whose daughter was Pramohinī; / of Suśīla, [the daughter was] Suśīlā, and of Svaravedin, [the daughter was] Susvarā;
Sutārā of Candrakānta, and Candrikā of Suprabha; / these are the excellent names of those apsarases, O king.
All those five were maidens, charming in their youth; / they always spoke to one another just like sisters.
As if emerged from the moon, they were brilliant like moonlight; / moon-faced and with lovely hair, they were radiant like moonstones.
Among the gods, these were playful maidens, like moonlight upon night-lotuses, / formed as a mass of loveliness, having divine forms and captivating the mind,
with expanding breasts like lotus buds, like ketakī blossoms in spring, / lovely with newly blossomed youth, like fresh sprouts in a forest of creepers,
fair as gold, with the radiance of gold, adorned with ornaments of gold, / wearing garlands of golden campaka blossoms, and finely dressed in gold-hued garments.
In musical scales, varieties of laughter, and various melodic fluctuations, / in the amusements of rhythmic instruments and playing the flute and vīṇā,
in the tempos of the lāsya dance mingled with the sounds of the mṛdaṅga drum, / in diversions such as painting, and in the arts, they were skilled.
Being such, those maidens charmed [all] with excellent play; / pampered by their fathers, they all wandered in the abode of Kubera.
Once, out of curiosity, the five maidens came together in the month of Mādhava, / gathering mandāra flowers from forest to forest.
To worship Gaurī, the celestial maidens once went to Lake Acchoda; / having gathered superior golden water-lilies from there, together with excellent blue lotuses,

and having bathed at the landing-place paved with pure lapis lazuli and crystal, and put on garments, / in silence they fashioned [an image of Gaurī] on an earthen altar-pedestal, adorned with gold and pearl ornaments.

Having worshipped Gaurī, anointed with sandal-paste, perfumes, and saffron, with choice lotuses and other offerings, / filled with auspicious devotional disposition by various offerings, the young maidens danced with performances of lāsya dance.

Relying on the celestial musical art, they then sang a melody with the highest note, / accompanied by modulating variations of natural vocal sounds; / those doe-eyed maidens sang with distinct syllables, rising high and melodious through their cadences.

While they were in that lovely state, their minds overflowing with joy from the shower of aesthetic delight, / the eldest son of the sage Vedanidhi arrived at that excellent sacred ford, Acchoda, to bathe.

Limitless in beauty, with an exquisite face, a youth with eyes as wide as blooming lotuses, / broad-chested, endowed with fine arms, exceptionally handsome, dark-complexioned, he was like a second Kāmadeva.

That celibate student looked splendid with his fine tuft of hair and his staff, like Manmatha with a bow; / clad in a black antelope skin, carrying a water jar, he wore a supreme girdle of muñja grass shining like gold around his waist.
Seeing that brāhmaṇa there on the bank of the lake, / the girls were filled with curiosity and rejoiced: “He shall be our guest!”
Abandoning their singing and dancing, eager to gaze upon him, / they were struck by Kāma with his arrows, like does by a hunter.
Saying, “Look! Look!” in flustered excitement, the five charming maidens / mistook that excellent young vipra for Kāmadeva himself.
Worshiping him again and again with their lotus-like eyes, / the apsarases then began to confer among themselves:
“If this is Kāmadeva, how could he be without Rati? / Or if he is one of the two Aśvins, those two always travel together.
Is he a gandharva, a kinnara, a siddha assuming form at will, / or some sage's son, or an exalted human being?
Or is this some god created by the Creator especially for us, / just as a treasure is revealed to a fortunate man by his past deeds?
So has this most excellent groom been brought to us maidens by Gaurī, / her heart softened by a wave of the water of compassion.
He is chosen by me!” “And by you!” “And by her!” / While the five maidens were speaking thus, O best of kings,
having completed his midday rites and heard their words, / the intelligent youth reflected: “What action would be meritorious [here]?
The son of Gādhi, Parāśara and others, Kaṇḍu, Devala, and other prominent twice-born men— / even those powerful yogins were easily enchanted by women; it is wondrous!
Struck by the sharp arrow-like eyes of women shot from the firm bow of their creeper-like brows, / released by the archer Makaraketu, whose deer-like mind would not fall?
Prudent judgment shines only so long, awe among people lasts only so long, / firmness of mind holds firm only so long, and regard for family remains only so long,
the power of austerity lasts only so long, and devotion to tranquility among men endures only so long, / until a man is intoxicated by the quickly stupefying wine that is the glance of women.
Women bewilder and intoxicate a passionate man with their lovely charms; / but me, who am devoted to preserving dharma, do they delight and intoxicate with their qualities?
Sensual men of thoroughly deluded minds imagine beauty / in the impure, worthless bodies of women, made of flesh, blood, feces, and urine, and become obsessed.
For women are declared cruel by the virtuous, pure-minded, and wise. / Before they draw near, I shall go home.”
Before those excellent women could come near him, / the twice-born vanished by the power of Viṣṇu.
When, by the power of his yoga, he disappeared from sight, O king, / seeing that wondrous deed of the Vaiṣṇava student of the Veda,
the maidens with frightened eyes, timid as does, / turned their blank gazes in all ten directions.
The maidens said: “He clearly knows sorcery, or else he understands illusion; / though seen, he has become unseen.” Thus they spoke to one another.
Their hearts were then consumed by the fire of separation, / just as an entire verdant forest is consumed by a blazing wildfire.
“Abandon your sorcerous art, beloved! Show yourself at once! / It was not fitting for you [to do] like a fly in the first mouthful [of food].
Alas, what pain! Why were you shown by the Creator, and from where were you fashioned? / Now it is known: you were created as our own cause of great torment!
Is your heart unfeeling? Do you have no regard for us? / Are you cruel, O beloved? Are you stealing away our minds?
Do you have no trust in us? Are you testing us? / Are you naturally detached? Are you skilled in magic?
Do you know the skillful science of entering into our hearts, / and yet do not know the way to exit? Why is this?”
Why are you truly angry with us when there is no offense? / Surely you do not know the sorrow, the deception caused to others!
Without seeing you, we are now ruined, O lord of our hearts! / We cannot live, or rather we live on only in the hope of seeing you again.
Take us quickly to that place where you have gone! / The Creator, stealing away the sight of you, has cut off the sprouts of our joy.
By all means grant us a sight of you! By all means have compassion! / Good people never look for an end [to their mercy] toward anyone.
Having thus lamented and waited for many moments, / those maidens then began to go home quickly out of fear of their father.
Bound by the chains of love for him, deeply agitated by separation, / somehow taking hold of courage, they returned to their respective homes.
Having arrived, all of them collapsed beside their mothers. / Asked by their mothers: “What is this? Why are you so late?”
[They replied:] “While we were tarrying, sporting together with the Kinnara women, / the day was not noticed by us at the Acchoda lake.
We are exhausted from the road, O mother; because of that there is a fever in our bodies. / Because of our great stupor, we do not have the heart to speak to anyone.”
Having spoken thus, the maidens rolled there upon the jeweled ground; / concealing their feelings, those innocent ones talked with their mothers.
One did not joyfully make her pet peacock dance then; / another, out of curiosity, did not teach speech to that parrot in the cage.
Another did not fondle her mongoose, nor coax her maina to speak; / another, utterly bewildered, did not play at all with the cranes.
They took no amusement; they did not revel in the palace; / they did not speak enough with their kinsmen; they did not play the vīṇā.
Whatever blossom of the wish-fulfilling tree was there seemed to them entirely like fire; / they did not drink the sweet honey fragrant with mandāra flowers.
Those maidens were just like female yogis with eyes fixed on the tip of their nose, / with an unbroken succession of imperceptible meditations, their minds fixed on the Supreme Person.
In a cavern shaded by moonstones and dripping with water, / staying for a moment at the window, for a moment in the bathhouse of water-fountains,
For a moment they arranged a couch of lotus leaves from the long pond, / being fanned by their companions with cool lotus leaves.
Thus those excellent women passed the night, which was like an entire cosmic age, / somehow holding on [to life], distraught as if afflicted with a fever.
In the morning, seeing the jewel of the sky [the sun] and considering it to be their very life, / having informed their respective mothers, they went to worship Gaurī.
Having bathed according to that rite, and having performed the worship / of the goddess with flowers and incenses, they remained there singing.
Meanwhile, that Brahmin also arrived from his father's hermitage / to bathe here in the Acchoda lake.
Just as lotus flowers [open] at the end of the night upon seeing the sun, / so the maidens' eyes blossomed upon seeing that young celibate student.
Having gone right there near the celibate student, / those maidens made a bond with their arms as a noose, left and right.
“You went away yesterday, beloved; today you cannot be allowed to go! / You have indeed been chosen by us; there is no deliberation about this for you.”
Addressed thus, the brāhmaṇa, laughing while held in the noose of their arms, said: / 'Gentle ladies, you speak agreeable, pleasing words.'
Yet, would not my vow be broken, who am established in the first stage of life? / The end [of study] has not been reached in the house of the guru by me who am devoted to the pursuit of knowledge.
In whatever stage of life one is, the dharma appropriate to it must be protected by the very wise. / Therefore I consider that this marriage is not dharma, O maidens.”
Having heard the Brahmin's words, the excellent women spoke to the Brahmin, / their voices full of longing in all notes, like cuckoos in the spring month of Mādhava:
“From dharma comes wealth, from wealth desire, and from desire the rise of the fruit of happiness; / thus the wise who know certainty describe it.
That desire has arisen before you out of an abundance of dharma. / Let it be enjoyed through various pleasures, for this place is pure.”
Hearing that speech of theirs, he spoke with a deep voice: / “Your speech is true, yet my vow is also mandatory.
Having obtained the permission of my guru, I shall perform the act of marriage, not otherwise.” / Addressed thus, they said again: “You are clearly a fool, O handsome one!

An effective medicine, an elixir with spiritual insight, accomplishment, a treasure, noble and excellent women, / a mantra, and an alchemical essence: these, when arrived through dharma, should be enjoyed by a wise man, O sage!
If an undertaking has by chance reached fulfillment, those who follow policy do not neglect it; / because neglect does not again yield fruit, therefore delay is never praised.
Even from poison, nectar should be accepted; even from filth, gold; / even from a lowborn person, highest knowledge; a jewel of a woman even from a base family.

Maidens of dense affection, pure by noble birth, their hearts moistened with tenderness, of sweet speech, choosing their own husband, / well-formed, of charming youth—only fortunate men obtain them here, not others.
Where are we, divine beauties, and where are you, an ascetic youth? / By this arrangement of what was difficult to unite, I consider that the Creator alone is clever.
Therefore, may you accept us now; may there be auspiciousness to you, / by the Gāndharva form of marriage; otherwise there is no living for us.”
Hearing this speech, the Brahmin, the best knower of dharma, then spoke: / “O deer-eyed ones, how can dharma be abandoned by men whose wealth is dharma?
Dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation: this quartet, / when practiced as prescribed, should be known as fruit-bearing; but when reversed, it is fruitless.
Being under a vow, I would not take a wife out of season. / One who does not know the proper time for an action does not attain the fruit of the action.
Since my mind is firmly attached to this deliberation of dharma, / therefore listen, O maidens, I do not desire a svayaṃvara.”
Knowing his intention thus, and having looked at one another, / releasing hand from hand, Pramohinī then seized his foot.
Suśīlā and Susvarā seized his arms; / Sutārā embraced him, and Candrikā kissed his face.
Even so, he was unmoved, like the fire of cosmic dissolution; / completely overwhelmed by anger, that celibate student cursed them:
“Since you have clung to me like female fiends, therefore you shall become female fiends!” / Cursed swiftly by him in this manner, leaving him, they stood before him:
“What sinful deed is this done by your action against the innocent? / Doing what is unpleasant to one who did what is pleasant—fie on you, the Death-god of dharma!
We have heard that for a man who commits betrayal against those who are in love, devoted, and friendly, / happiness in both worlds comes to ruin.
Therefore, by our curse you too quickly become a fiend!” / Even having spoken thus, those girls sighed, overcome with wrath.
At that very lake, O king, out of mutual fury, / those maidens and the celibate student all attained the state of fiends.
He as a fiend and they as female fiends, weeping most dreadfully, / exhaust the karmic fruitions of the deed previously accumulated.
What was previously accumulated, good and bad, prevails indeed at its proper time, / unavoidable like one's own shadow, even for the gods, O king.
Their fathers and their mothers weep here and there, / and so do the brothers of the girls; for destiny is indeed hard to overcome.
Henceforth, those piśācas, exceedingly distressed in search of food, / running here and there, dwell on the shore of the lake.

3.23.m: Nārada said: / After a long time had thus passed, Lomaśa, the best of sages, / an illustrious sage wandering at his own pleasure, arrived there.
Seeing that brāhmaṇa, all the piśācas, afflicted with hunger, / assembled as a horde and rushed forward, wishing to devour him.
Yet scorched by Lomaśa's fierce radiant energy, / unable to stand before him, they all stayed far away.
Then, by the force of his past deeds, that twice-born who had become a piśāca, / seeing Lomaśa, O king, prostrated himself with eight limbs [touching the ground],
and spoke true and pleasant words, folding his hands at his head: / 'Only when great fortune arises, O vipra, does the company of the virtuous occur.
Between a person who constantly bathes in holy places like the Gaṅgā, / and one who keeps the company of the good, the company of the good is superior.
The company of teachers, O vipra, yields visible and invisible fruits on earth; / it grants heaven, removes disease, and what is more, dispels darkness.'
Having said this, he narrated that wondrous past event: / 'These are Gandharva maidens, O sage, and I am the son of a twice-born.'
All of us, in the form of piśācas, deluded by our mutual curse, / stand before you with miserable faces, O best of sages.
Will there be no deliverance for these youngsters from the sight of you? / Can a mass of darkness really remain in the sky at the rising of the sun?'
Hearing this speech, Lomaśa, his mind softened with compassion, / that one of great radiance replied to the sorrowful son of the sage:
'By my grace, let memory arise at once for all of you, / and let it abide in dharma, so that your mutual curse may dissolve.'
The piśāca said: / 'O great sage, declare that dharma by which I may be freed from sin! / This is not a time for delay, since the fire of the curse is terrible.'
Lomaśa said: / 'Perform a bath in the Revā with me according to the rules; / the Revā will free you from the curse, for there is no other expiation.
Listen attentively, O twice-born: the destruction of sins for men / is surely produced by bathing in the Revā; such is my resolved conviction.
Sin committed across seven lives, as well as present wrongdoing, / a bath in the Revā burns up completely, as fire does a pile of cotton.
The sin for which [scriptures] perceive no expiation, O piśāca, / all that is destroyed merely by bathing in the waters of the Narmadā.
A bath in the Narmadā produces knowledge; therefore, indeed, it bears the fruit of liberation. / The holy places of the Himavat truly remove all sins;
indeed, this one that grants Indra's world was fashioned by those who expound the Veda. / The Revā is proclaimed to yield all desires and to grant liberation.
Slaying sin, removing sin, bestowing the fruit of all desires, / immersion in the Narmadā destroys sin and grants the world of Viṣṇu.
Immersion in the Yamunā is best for [attaining] the world of the sun; / that in the Sarasvatī destroys sins and grants the fruit of Brahmā's world.
The Viśālā is proclaimed to give vast fruit, O piśāca; / it is a forest fire to the fuel of sins, taking away deeds that cause rebirth.
Immersion in the Narmadā is proclaimed to lead to Viṣṇu's world and to liberation. / The Sarayū, the Gaṇḍakī, the Sindhu, the Candrabhāgā, the Kauśikī,
the Tāpī, the Godāvarī, the Bhīmā, the Payoṣṇī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇikā, / the Kāverī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and other rivers flowing to the ocean—

among them the Revā is declared supreme, the bestower of the world of Viṣṇu. / But the Revā is reached through merits performed in past lives, O twice-born; / plunging in it, O son of a sage, grants freedom from rebirth.
The gods dwelling in heaven always sing: "When will the Revā come into our sight, / where bathed humans do not experience the agony of the womb, and remain in the presence of Viṣṇu?"
Those humans who dive daily into the waters of the Revā, though covered by many sins, / do not sink into hells by virtue of dharma, but roam beautifully in heaven like gods.

In ancient times, the Creator weighed the Revā on a scale against severe vows, charity, austerities, and sacrifices; / of the two, O piśāca, the Revā quickly proved superior, the bringer of liberation.'
Nārada said: / Hearing this word of Lomaśa, the piśācas / went swiftly with him to plunge into the Revā.
Then, by destiny, a wind arose on the bank of the Revā, / bringing drops of water onto their bodies touched by the current.
From the touch of drops of Revā water, they were freed from their piśāca state; / instantly attaining divine forms, they praised the Narmadā.
Then, by Lomaśa's instruction, those Gandharva maidens / were happily married by that twice-born on the bank of the Narmadā.
He dwelt there for a very long time, bathing, drinking, and plunging in its waters, / and having worshipped the Narmadā there, they went to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus has been related to you, O king, this most meritorious legendary history / based on the virtues of the Narmadā, destroying sins upon being heard.

3.24.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Now tell me of other holy places spoken of by Vasiṣṭha, / by hearing of which sins go to dissolution, O Nārada.
Nārada said: / Listen to the holy places spoken of by Vasiṣṭha here, O king: / having reached the southern sea, chaste and with senses conquered,
one obtains the [fruit of an] Agniṣṭoma and ascends a celestial chariot. / Having reached the Carmaṇvatī, disciplined and with regulated food,
permitted by Rantideva, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma. / Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to Arbuda, the son of the Himavat,
where in ancient times there was an opening in the earth, O Yudhiṣṭhira; / there is the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned in the three worlds.
Staying there for one night, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. / Having touched the water at the Piṅgā holy place, chaste, O ruler of men,
one obtains the fruit of a hundred brown cows, O tiger among men. / Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to Prabhāsa, renowned in the world,
where the fire-god himself is eternally present, / the mouth of the deities, O hero, the fire having the wind as its charioteer.
Having bathed in that excellent holy place, pure and of restrained mind, / a person obtains the fruit of both the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
Going thence to the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, / having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows, one is exalted in the heavenly world.
Shining eternally like fire with radiance, O bull of the Bharatas, / having bathed with restrained mind in the holy place of the king of waters,
having dwelt there for three nights, one should offer libations to the ancestors and gods; / he shines like Soma and gains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice.
Then one should go to the Varadāna holy place, O best of the Bharatas, / where a boon was given to Viṣṇu by Durvāsas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
